reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: Popliteal venous entrapment is dynamic or fixed compression of the popliteal vein within the popliteal fossa, usually by an anomalous or hypertrophied medial head of gastrocnemius or by a fibrous band, and it frequently coexists with popliteal artery entrapment

It characteristically affects young, athletic adults and presents with exertional or positional calf swelling, heaviness, aching and sometimes venous claudication, typically provoked by active plantarflexion or dorsiflexion
It should be considered in unexplained deep vein thrombosis or leg swelling in a young patient who lacks conventional thrombotic risk factors
Provocative duplex ultrasound with the ankle in active plantar- and dorsiflexion is the key first-line test, showing reduced or abolished popliteal venous flow on the manoeuvre
Cross-sectional imaging by MRI or MR venography, or by CT, defines the musculotendinous anatomy and distinguishes an anatomical anomaly from purely functional (positional) entrapment
Care is needed to separate true entrapment from the physiological compression that can occur in normal limbs during extreme plantarflexion, so as to avoid overdiagnosis

Symptomatic anatomical entrapment is treated surgically by decompression, releasing the offending muscle slip or fibrous band, whereas functional entrapment without a structural anomaly is generally managed more conservatively
reference.pathophysiology: The popliteal vein normally traverses the popliteal fossa alongside the artery, passing between the heads of gastrocnemius. In entrapment, an anomalous origin or accessory slip of the medial head of gastrocnemius, a fibrous band, or muscular hypertrophy compresses the vein, particularly during muscle contraction in plantarflexion or with certain knee positions. Repetitive compression produces intermittent venous outflow obstruction, venous hypertension and stasis, which give rise to exertional swelling and predispose to intimal injury and secondary thrombosis. In functional entrapment, hypertrophied but normally positioned muscles compress otherwise normal vessels, so imaging at rest may be unremarkable while provocative manoeuvres reveal the obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Deep vein thrombosis of another cause
Chronic venous insufficiency with venous reflux
Popliteal (Baker) cyst or popliteal venous aneurysm
Musculoskeletal calf pathology such as gastrocnemius strain
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound with provocative plantar- and dorsiflexion manoeuvres
MRI or MR venography of the popliteal fossa to display the musculotendinous anatomy
CT venography as an alternative for anatomical assessment
Positional contrast venography in selected cases
Assessment of the popliteal artery for coexisting arterial entrapment using ankle-brachial index and arterial duplex
Thrombophilia screen when the patient presents with deep vein thrombosis
Cross-sectional imaging to exclude an alternative popliteal mass such as a cyst or aneurysm
redFlags: Deep vein thrombosis in a young patient without conventional risk factors
Coexisting arterial entrapment with claudication or limb ischaemia
Recurrent thrombosis or post-thrombotic changes despite anticoagulation
Progressive symptoms that increasingly limit activity
reference.prognosis: With timely surgical decompression of an anatomical entrapment, symptomatic and functional outcomes are generally good. Delayed diagnosis may lead to established deep vein thrombosis, post-thrombotic syndrome and chronic venous insufficiency.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing entrapment from the physiological venous compression seen in normal limbs on extreme plantarflexion
Missing the diagnosis in young patients with unexplained deep vein thrombosis or exertional leg swelling
Failing to assess for a coexisting popliteal artery entrapment
Relying on resting, non-provocative imaging, which may appear normal
Treating recurrent deep vein thrombosis with anticoagulation alone without addressing the underlying compression
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
European Society for Vascular Surgery clinical practice guidance on popliteal entrapment
management: Surgical decompression by dividing the anomalous or hypertrophied medial head of gastrocnemius or the constricting fibrous band relieving the popliteal vein, the definitive treatment for anatomical entrapment
Venous repair or reconstruction where the vein wall is already damaged or thrombosed
Anticoagulation when entrapment has precipitated a secondary deep vein thrombosis
Graduated compression and activity modification for symptom relief and in mild or purely functional cases where surgery is not warranted
Assessment for and treatment of coexisting popliteal artery entrapment
Referral to vascular surgery, with care to distinguish true entrapment from physiological compression so as to avoid unnecessary operation
